utterances.text: I don't have the total figure. Just like you, I can look at the numbers of the 1991 census to arrive at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Although in a number of places in your report you mentioned assessments and assumptions, you cannot tell us how many Croats there were in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: You do the calculation. 87.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 78.1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report deals with displaced persons in the war-affected areas of Croatia. Not the whole of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So, in 1991 if there were 3 and a half million Croats out of which 220.000 were expelled, what is the percentage?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Well, you do your math.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I will. Just a few more questions, Ms. Radic. Do you have any records of how many Croatian citizens were expelled after Operations Flash and Storm?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Given that most of those people left Croatia, there is no precise -- there are no precise figures. We have precise information about those figures registered in the Croatian Danubian region in 1997. Between April 1997 and April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Radic, Your Honour, I believe my question was clear. I would kindly ask that my question be answered, if possible. I don't think it was confusing. My question is, how many people were driven out after Operations Flash and Storm, do you or do you not know that? Do you have records of that?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us why not?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: How could we keep any records when people were not in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were these Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Most of them were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Under your legal definition, did they fall in the displaced persons category?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: According to the legal definition I have explained, most of them became refugees because they went abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reasons for which they left Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No. I think this is a completely separate issue from those discussed here. We need to go into something that amounts to opinions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrovic, I believe that you have put this question to the witness at several instances and Ms. Radic has said that she was not in a position to answer this question. Also, I would like to point out that when you put this question and you said after the Operation Storm, you were in a way answering this question as well as putting the question to the witness, and that the reasons seemed to be quite obvious, even if they are not in the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand your remark. Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The area discussed here, was it also affected by the war? The areas where Operations Storm and Flash took place?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, those areas were also defined as UNPA areas and areas of special state concern. These are all the same areas in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Jordash, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just take brief instructions, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Friedman, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just now, Ms. Radic, you were asked by Mr. Petrovic whether you had figures on the Serbs that left Croatia, and your answer was, and I quote: "How could we keep any records when people were not in Croatia." And then you began to explain that you did register when they returned. And so could you clarify, please, in 1997 whether Serbs were entitled to the same returnee status that Croats were entitled to?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: Precisely. We kept records of those Serbs who returned to the Republic of Croatia. We used the same forms shown here in order to take their statements and keep the statistics. In 1997, in addition to those who returned to Croatia, we also registered those who were accommodated in the Croatian Danubian region during UNPA administration. This was the UN transitional administration which was concluded on the 15th of January, 1998. We registered them then. There were 31.000 people accommodated in the Croatian Danubian region and another 4 and a half thousand persons who came from Serbia and had themselves registered in the Croatian Danubian region in order to be able to go back to their homes. We used the very same form, the same method as we did when registering DPs and refugees in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have one question to put to you, Ms. Radic. I was wondering about the registration form for displaced persons or refugees. I was wondering whether they were filled in on a voluntary basis, how did it work? If someone was moved to another region were they freely filling in this form? Did they have to register themselves or could they just live with members of the family without anybody knowing about them having moved from one region to another?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: No one was under any obligation to be registered, but most of the people did. Of course, there are always exceptions and people did so for their personal reasons. But most people did have themselves registered for one single reason, they had no place to be accommodated or receive food otherwise. They had been left without property and source of income. One of the basic reasons for registering was the economic one. They were left without anything overnight, hence they needed accommodation and food, which, in this case, was provided by the state. For the state to be able to do so, records had to be kept about those people. All people who had themselves registered in that way, were put in the same database that was used to keep records of allowances given to people for private accommodation and how many of them were in organised accommodation facilities. You can see in the tables. For example in 1993, 120.000 people were housed in organised accommodation facilities in displaced persons settlements, hotels, and other facilities of that type. Out of that figure, 85.000 were displaced persons. In order to keep files and registers of those people, we knew -- we had to know the precise numbers. People who were able to cope in other ways by finding accommodation with friends and relatives were under no obligation to have themselves registered. However, most people did because otherwise they had no other source of income. The only income was to receive an allowance from the state and accommodation as well as food. When you are a refugee or displaced person, you have nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This is very [indiscernible]. Yes, Mr. Petrovic. I believe you have another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two brief questions by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Radic, what is the percentage of the Serbs who had fled Croatia who returned until the present day?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: I told you the figure, 126.000. That's the official information from the same data. That's the latest piece of information we have. It's very difficult to compare though because the census was done in 2001, I don't have official information here, maybe it's somewhere in my notes, but after that another 60.000 Serbs returned and had themselves registered upon return to Croatia. So we are now awaiting the next census next year to be able to tell you what the precise number of those living in Croatia today is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another brief question: What was the percentage of Serbs, according to the census of 2001, lived in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANNA MARIA RADIC
utterances.text: The percentage was 4 and a half per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would like to know whether additional questions have created some further questions to be put to the witness? Apparently not. So, Ms. Radic, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to present your report and to answer the questions put by the parties and I wish you a very safe trip back home. The trial stands adjourned and we will resume our hearing until Monday, 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
